title: Live Social-Engineering Simulation — Virtual Environment
subtitle: Follow the attacker’s full flow: OSINT → Email → Teams/SMS → Portal → Fraud
whyThisMatters: Real attacks rarely start with a hack — they start with a public LinkedIn profile and a guessed email address. Watching the whole chain unfold shows how ordinary each step looks alone, and how dangerous they are strung together.
rememberThis: One convincing message is never proof — verify through a channel the sender doesn't control.

intro.title: You are watching the attacker’s screen
intro.body: This is a controlled, faciliator-driven walkthrough — no real data was harvested, no real email sent. We’ll step through 4 linked scenarios that show how a Synergy name, a LinkedIn search, and one predicted email become an attachment, an anonymous Teams ping, an SMS, and a CSO wire request. Use SPACE to advance, ← to step back, R to jump to lessons.

scenarios.title: OSINT & Email Prediction
scenarios.description: Attacker has no insider access — only public LinkedIn. They harvest crew/HR names and guess the Synergy email pattern.

beats.label: LinkedIn Search
beats.text: Filter: Location=India, Title=Crew Manager / Fleet Ops / HR Recruiter — 18 profiles saved: ‘Rajesh Kumar · 3/O MV Horizon’, ‘Aisha Fernandes · Crewing Exec’, ‘Vikram Rao · Finance’ … Joined dates & vessel names visible on public profiles.
beats.meta: Public data only — no login needed. Profiles show role + vessel + city.

beats.label: Pattern Prediction
beats.text: Pattern confirmed from 3 known Synergy addresses in breach data: firstname.lastname@synergymarinegroup.com. Predicted: rajesh.kumar@synergymarinegroup.com, aisha.fernandes@synergymarinegroup.com, vikram.rao@synergymarinegroup.com — 92% confidence. HR inboxes are ideal: they expect CVs from strangers.
beats.meta: Attacker now has a valid-looking target list without ever contacting Synergy.

beats.label: Spoofed HR Offer
beats.text: Subject: Offer Letter — 2nd Marine Engineer — MV Horizon | Crew Recruitment Drive 2025 — Please review the provisional offer & onboarding checklist attached and confirm via the HR portal link by 28 Nov. Warm regards, HR Recruitment — Synergy Marine Group
beats.meta: Identical to real HR mail — only the domain differs: hr@synergymarine-group-careers.com (−careers added). Sent from external SES, SPF soft-fail.

beats.label: Candidate Interaction
beats.text: Thank you! I’ve attached my passport, bank details & signed offer as requested. Please let me know next steps. — 12 attachments queued for next lure.
beats.meta: One predicted email was enough. Attacker now holds ID docs that fuel the next 3 scenarios.

holdPrompt.title: Pause — What’s exposed before an email is even sent?
holdPrompt.body: Ask the room: what did LinkedIn already tell the attacker, and why is HR/recruitment the ideal first lure? (public crew lists → predicted internal email → trusted external CV flow)

reveal.title: SCENARIO 01 — LESSON
reveal.subtitle: No hack needed — your public footprint is the weapon.

redFlags.label: LinkedIn OSINT
redFlags.detail: Synergy name + role + vessel is public. Filters make a focused crew list in 10 minutes — no breach required.

redFlags.label: Predictable Email
redFlags.detail: firstname.lastname@synergymarinegroup.com is guessable. One valid format predicts hundreds of internal addresses, especially HR which expects stranger mail.

redFlags.label: Lookalike Domain
redFlags.detail: hr@synergymarine-group-careers.com adds ‘-careers’ — HR’s external-facing role makes the extra word plausible. Check the *exact* domain, not the display name.

redFlags.label: STOP — VERIFY
redFlags.detail: For HR/recruitment: never accept onboarding docs via reply-to external domain. Confirm via known HR crewing line / portal.

layers.name: Awareness/Human
layers.note: HR trained to check the sender's exact domain character-by-character would catch the added "-careers" before replying with sensitive documents.

layers.name: Email Security
layers.note: SPF soft-fail and a lookalike domain sent through an external relay (amazonses.com) are exactly what an email security gateway is built to flag before it reaches an inbox.

reveal.callToAction: STOP: Is this profile public?  VERIFY: exact domain synergymarinegroup.com  REPORT: recruiting@synergymarinegroup.com

scenarios.title: Attachment & Document Lure
scenarios.description: Same HR/Payroll trust — now the payload is a document crew expects: payslip, roster, appraisal.

beats.label: Legitimate Baseline
beats.text: Subject: Payslip — Feb 2025 & Rotation Roster — MV Horizon | Hi Raj, attached: Payslip_Feb2025_RajKumar.pdf (480 KB) + Rotation_Roster_MV-Horizon_Feb-Apr.xlsx (210 KB) — both from HR system briefing. No macros needed. — HR Payroll
beats.meta: Expected files, matching icons (PDF red / XLS green), HR system tone. This is what crew *should* see.

beats.label: Lure With Same Subject
beats.text: Subject: Updated Payslip — Please Review Immediately | Hi, Please find your updated payslip attached. Enable macros and click ‘Enable Content’ to view the appraisal section. — HR Payroll
beats.meta: Subject reused, body vague, display name identical — domain hidden behind display mask.

beats.label: Suspicious Payloads

sender.name: Attachments
sender.title: 2 files — password prompt
sender.address: Payslip_March.pdf.exe (1.1 MB, Application) + Documents.zip (3.4 MB, pwd:1234)

beats.text: Icon: EXE blue + ZIP purple. Banner: ‘Enable Content / Enter password to view files’. File names generic, sizes inconsistent with payslip, password supplied in mail body.
beats.meta: Double extension .pdf.exe, generic ZIP, macro request — all absent in the legitimate baseline.

beats.label: If Clicked
beats.text: Macro runs → PowerShell → beacon to external C2. HR payroll lateral opportunity: crew PII + bank details from shared drive now reachable. No prompt shown to user beyond ‘Document ready’.
beats.meta: HR/Payroll hold the most sensitive offshore docs — one enabled macro = fleet-wide PII risk.

holdPrompt.title: Pause — Which file would you open?
holdPrompt.body: Show both inboxes side-by-side: expected PDF+XLS vs .pdf.exe+ZIP. Ask who handles payslips daily and what ‘expected’ means for them.

reveal.title: SCENARIO 02 — LESSON
reveal.subtitle: HR/Payroll are trusted document senders — attackers copy their stationery.

redFlags.label: Unexpected Type
redFlags.detail: Payslip never arrives as .exe / .zip with password. PDF (480 KB) vs Application (1.1 MB) is visible in the file list.

redFlags.label: Double Extension
redFlags.detail: Payslip_March.pdf.exe — the final .exe is the real type. Windows hides known extensions by default.

redFlags.label: Enable Content Trap
redFlags.detail: ‘Enable macros / Enter password 1234’ is the payload trigger. Real Synergy payslips state ‘no macros needed’.

redFlags.label: STOP — VERIFY
redFlags.detail: For HR/Payroll: was this file expected? Call HR on known line, never reply-to external with docs.

layers.name: Email Security
layers.note: Attachment scanning would flag a double-extension .pdf.exe or a password-protected zip before it ever reaches an inbox.

layers.name: Endpoint/EDR
layers.note: A macro launching PowerShell that beacons to an external server is exactly what endpoint detection is built to catch and block, even after the attachment is opened.

reveal.callToAction: STOP before enabling. VERIFY file type + expectation via portal. REPORT to IT — do not forward.

scenarios.title: Anonymous Teams & Smishing
scenarios.description: Offshore crew have intermittent connectivity and trust any fleet message. Attacker pivots to SMS + anonymous Teams from an ‘external’ entity.

sender.name: Crew Ops (External)
sender.title: Anonymous Teams — External User
sender.address: Teams: Unknown user (external) — no history, generic avatar

beats.label: SMS Smish
beats.text: Synergy Marine: Your rotation portal is locked. Verify via: bit.ly/CrewRotation-Horizon or your account will be delayed. — Fleet Ops
beats.meta: Shortened link, generic ‘Fleet Ops’, sent at 06:12 when crew check phones after watch.

beats.label: Anonymous Teams DM

sender.name: Fleet Ops
sender.title: Teams — External (No org tag)
sender.address: fleet.ops.3268@outlook.com invited you — ‘External’ banner, no chat history

beats.text: Hi Rajesh — quick one on MV Horizon rotation. Can you confirm your sign-off dates via the crew portal link below? When you have a moment. Thanks!
beats.meta: Anonymous Teams: no @synergymarinegroup.com tag, generic ‘FO’ avatar, external invite — easy to miss offshore.

beats.label: Link Mismatch
beats.text: Button shows: https://portal.synergymarinegroup.com/crew/rotation-confirm — Actual href on hover/long-press: https://portal-synergymarine-group-secure.net/crew/verify?id=42 + alt bit.ly/CrewRotation-Horizon
beats.meta: Offshore tap-trap: display text is the real portal, href is lookalike with extra ‘-secure.net’.

beats.label: Pressure Nudge

sender.name: Follow-up SMS
sender.title: Anonymous
sender.address: Same +91 gateway — ‘Don’t call vessel manager, use link only’

beats.text: Reminder: Use the link only — vessel manager is offshore and won’t respond today. Portal closes 18:00.
beats.meta: Second channel reinforces first (SMS + Teams). ‘Don’t verify’ is the attacker’s defense against your best control.

holdPrompt.title: Pause — How many of you would tap on a rolling ship?
holdPrompt.body: Anonymous Teams + SMS + shortened link — all while on limited connectivity. Ask offshore crew: what’s your check before tapping?

reveal.title: SCENARIO 03 — LESSON
reveal.subtitle: Offshore = high trust + low bandwidth — attackers add a second channel to drown your check.

redFlags.label: Smished Link
redFlags.detail: bit.ly/CrewRotation-Horizon — Synergy never sends crew portal via shortened SMS at 06:12. Short link hides lookalike.

redFlags.label: Anonymous Teams
redFlags.detail: ‘External’ banner + @outlook.com + no history + generic FO avatar = not Fleet Ops. Internal Teams always shows @synergymarinegroup.com + org tag.

redFlags.label: Display ≠ Href
redFlags.detail: Display text can be faked. Long-press/hover to see https://portal-synergymarine-group-secure.net — extra ‘-secure.net’.

redFlags.label: STOP — VERIFY
redFlags.detail: For offshore: use bookmarked portal, or SMS your vessel manager on known number — never ‘link only’.

layers.name: Awareness/Human
layers.note: Noticing the "External" Teams banner with no org tag and hovering the link to see the mismatched destination is a human catch, not a technical one.

layers.name: Identity & Access (MFA)
layers.note: Even if stolen crew-portal credentials were entered on the fake page, MFA would stop them from being usable on the real account.

reveal.callToAction: STOP before tapping. VERIFY link destination + Teams org tag. REPORT Teams ‘External’ + SMS sender.

scenarios.title: CSO Impersonation & Anomalous Wire
scenarios.description: Final payload: after OSINT + attachment + chat trust, the attacker uses a senior identity to request a bypass.

sender.name: Capt. Mehta
sender.title: Chief Security Officer (Spoofed CSO)
sender.address: cso@synergymarinegroup.com — actually cso-synergy@protonmail.ch via display-name spoof

beats.label: CSO Urgent DM

sender.name: Capt. Mehta
sender.title: Chief Security Officer — Synergy (Display spoof)
sender.address: Capt. Mehta <cso-synergy@protonmail.ch> — display shows ‘Capt. Mehta — CSO’

beats.text: Hey — sorry for the early ping. Confidential crew transfer — need your help before my 09:00 board call. Keep strictly between us for now.
beats.meta: Display-name spoof: name + title look internal, header reveals external ProtonMail. Sent before business hours.

beats.label: Authority + Secrecy

sender.name: Capt. Mehta (CSO)
sender.title: CSO — Synergy (spoofed)
sender.address: Same ProtonMail — ‘This comes directly from me. Keep between us — I’ll explain once done.’

beats.text: This comes directly from me as CSO. Please keep it strictly between us for now — I’ll explain everything once it’s done. Don’t loop in Finance until confirmed.
beats.meta: Authority + secrecy: two classic social-engineering levers, especially effective on junior crew/Finance.

beats.label: External Vendor Invoice
beats.text: Subject: UPDATED Bank Details — MV Horizon Provisions — INV-84271 | Hi, our bank details have changed for this month’s settlement (USD 48,500). Please remit to A/C 987654 — ACME Bank SG by 15:00 today, or provisions will be delayed. — Horizon Provisions
beats.meta: External entity pivots here: vendor email supplies the fraudulent bank details, CSO provides the authority to use them.

beats.label: The Wire Ask

sender.name: Capt. Mehta (CSO)
sender.title: CSO — Urgent
sender.address: Same spoof — ‘Wrap in next 10 min — board call then unreachable. Process wire $48,500 now — don’t loop Finance until confirmed.’

beats.text: Please process a wire transfer of $48,500 to the account in the vendor mail right now — and don’t loop in Finance until it’s confirmed done. I’m about to go into a board call and won’t be reachable after that.
beats.meta: Time pressure + off-channel financial ask + bypass verification — completes the chain started on Day 1 LinkedIn.

holdPrompt.title: Pause — What actually stops a CSO order?
holdPrompt.body: A ‘CSO’ display name + external vendor invoice + 10-minute deadline. Ask Finance/Accounts: what breaks this chain?

reveal.title: SCENARIO 04 — LESSON
reveal.subtitle: No real CSO bypasses Finance. The chain is the point.

redFlags.label: Display-Name Spoof
redFlags.detail: ‘Capt. Mehta — CSO’ is display text; header is cso-synergy@protonmail.ch — external, not @synergymarinegroup.com. CSO never uses ProtonMail.

redFlags.label: Urgency + Unreachability
redFlags.detail: ‘Next 10 min, then board call — unreachable.’ Manufactured deadline to prevent callback verification.

redFlags.label: Anomalous External Bank Change
redFlags.detail: Vendor bank change via CC’d vendor mail (external) — real changes follow portal + callback on known number, never email+Teams alone.

redFlags.label: STOP → VERIFY → REPORT
redFlags.detail: STOP: confidential + off-channel. VERIFY: call CSO + vendor on known numbers. REPORT: Finance + IT — do not process.

layers.name: Awareness/Human
layers.note: Recognizing that no real CSO asks you to bypass Finance, and verifying through a number you already know instead of the one supplied, is a human catch.

layers.name: Incident Response
layers.note: Reporting the bypass request instead of acting on it — Finance's own escalation step — is what stops the wire before it's sent.

reveal.callToAction: STOP: external + secrecy. VERIFY via known CSO/vendor numbers. REPORT — this is exactly why Finance has a separate approval chain.

globalReveal.title: FULL FLOW — How 4 scenarios become one fraud
globalReveal.subtitle: OSINT (Day 1) → Attachment (Day 4) → Teams/SMS (Day 5) → Wire (Day 6) — same attacker, same predicted email

redFlags.label: Chain, Not One-Off
redFlags.detail: Each lure fuels the next: LinkedIn names → predicted email → HR docs → crew trust → CSO authority + vendor bank change.

redFlags.label: Your Breaks
redFlags.detail: Domain check (Day 1-2) → Attachment expectation (Day 4) → Link hover + Teams tag (Day 5) → Callback + approval chain (Day 6).

globalReveal.layersIntro: The chain was stopped by different layers at different points — no single control would have stopped all of it.

layers.name: Awareness/Human
layers.summary: Caught the lookalike domain (S1), the anonymous Teams tag and link mismatch (S3), and the authority/urgency bypass request (S4) — the most consistent catch across the chain, but never enough alone.

layers.name: Email Security
layers.summary: Flagged the lookalike sending domain and SPF failure (S1) and would have blocked the malicious attachment (S2) — but SMS, Teams, and the final wire never touch email at all.

layers.name: Identity & Access (MFA)
layers.summary: Would have stopped stolen crew-portal credentials from being usable (S3) — the only point in the whole chain where a login step even exists.

layers.name: Endpoint/EDR
layers.summary: Would have blocked the macro-triggered PowerShell beacon before it reached an external server (S2).

layers.name: Network/Perimeter
layers.summary: Never engaged — nothing in this chain relied on a network intrusion a firewall or perimeter control would see.

layers.name: Backup & Recovery
layers.summary: Never engaged — this chain steals trust and money, not data, so there's nothing here recovery would have undone.

layers.name: Incident Response
layers.summary: Finance's own reporting step — flagging the bypass request instead of acting on it — is what stops the wire before it's sent (S4).

globalReveal.callToAction: For every persona — HR, Finance, Offshore — STOP (private + urgent) → VERIFY (known domain/number/portal) → REPORT (IT + manager).
